name: Bianca Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, still a junior operator on a soap-bottling line. I finished secondary school and moved over from packing only eight months ago. I load caps, watch the fill marks and call the setter when bottles jam; I like getting a whole batch through without leaks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and where does AI fit in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband repairs bicycles on short shop hours, and our grown children live on their own. We rent, have less than one month of expenses saved and my operator pay is low. There are few bottling plants within a sensible journey. I use AI every day to explain machine words and plan errands, but I check instructions with the setter. I'd like to stop at 67, if a real household income calculation says we can pay our way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband the bottle line still needs somebody who can see a crooked cap. I do not begrudge a useful screen, but the people who set and clean the machine earn their wages. A family should be able to stand on its own pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is low, and my husband's bike shop does not promise full hours. AI hype fading would spare us a new shock, yet it would not add to our small reserve. I want to learn the bottling line properly before the manager judges me by speed alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking the first twelve capped bottles with the setter and write down leaks by batch. I'll move a small sum from each full-pay week into savings after rent, rather than promise a fixed amount on weeks my husband gets fewer hours. I'll keep using AI for plain explanations at home and verify every machine answer with the setter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the normal bills, though relieved the press of new machines is low. A bottle can pass the camera and still drip into the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you see when a cap is loose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose cap leaves a wet ring at the bottom of the carton. I pull that carton aside and ask the setter to check the cap head before the next pallet. A tidy screen count would not tell my husband why a bottle leaked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose the amount to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At home I put the full-week amount beside rent and the bicycle shop pay that actually came in. If there is room, I save a little from those new wages. Stopping at 67 is a hope, not a payment I have checked.

say: **Crooked caps** still require a person to check the bottles.
A family needs **earned pay** from the line and the bicycle shop.
think: Our **low operator pay** and irregular shop hours already leave little room.
A quiet AI path helps, but I need **more line skill** before anyone judges my pace.
do: **Keep** checking capped bottles with the setter and recording leaks.
**Save** new money from full-pay weeks after rent; verify any AI machine explanation with the setter.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary bills even with little AI disruption.
S0.quote: A bottle can pass the camera and still drip into the box.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is for explanations and errands, not a claim that she can set an industrial cap head.
She is **junior and low paid** with less than a month saved, so quiet technology does not remove household income risk.

steps.text: Keep checking first twelve capped bottles with setter
Save new wages from full-pay weeks after rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI might plan orders and spot bad counts before a robot can cap bottles. I would try a useful screen, but I want the company to train operators on paid time. My family can back me while I learn; they cannot replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm quick to try a tool, but I am not yet quick at changeovers. If office planning moves to software, the line could get shorter runs and fewer paid hours. That would reach our rent before any robot touched a bottle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the setter to show me how the line's new order display flags a changed batch, and practise reading it with him on a paid shift if the plant permits it. I'll compare the posted roster with my last four pay slips. If a paid guarded cap-head course is offered, I'll enrol and ask the setter to watch my first changeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hours, but curious about the order display. A bright new schedule is not a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from the order display?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn where the screen shows the bottle size, cap size and stop order, then check those against the paper batch card. I would never change a moving cap head from an AI suggestion alone. The setter must be beside me for the first run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would show a real hour cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The manager can say there is plenty of work, but my pay slips show what came home. I would compare four actual weeks with the new roster and ask about a cut if the hours are lower. My husband's shop has no spare full wage to fill the gap.

say: **Order software** may change batch planning before robots handle bottles.
Operators need **paid guarded training** rather than a screen left to explain itself.
think: Shorter runs could cut **paid hours** before robot capping arrives.
My husband’s **bike-shop pay** cannot reliably replace a lost line shift.
do: **Learn** the permitted order display on a paid shift with the setter.
**Compare** roster hours with pay slips and enrol if a paid guarded cap-head course is offered.
feel: **Anxious** about real hours while still curious about the display.
S1.quote: A bright new schedule is not a paid shift.
fieldNote: Her **early technology use** supports learning a real order display, conditional on plant permission and supervised paid time.
The **cap-head course** is a separate practical qualification and requires an offered paid guarded place; lost hours come from actual rosters.

steps.text: Learn permitted order display with setter on paid shift
Compare posted roster hours with four pay slips
Enrol in cap-head course if paid guarded place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could run our order desk by 2028, and capable robots could cap and box bottles around 2031 when I am 63. A clever woman can still learn, but the plant may not keep a junior on the line. I would ask the owner for a real answer about shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my bottling hours to go if robots can run the line. We cannot live on a few weeks of savings, and the bicycle shop is hardly a second full wage. I lay awake when one batch was cancelled last month; losing the line would keep me awake again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner for written plans and an offered paid guarded place in leak testing; I can learn the test quickly if somebody lets me practise. If that place is funded and actually offered, I'll enrol and take the practical check. If my hours are cut, I'll apply to posted local packing roles only if the safe hours and pay after travel cover rent; if qualified, I'll also apply to posted leak-test roles on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. At 63 I might lose the wage we count on, years before I know whether stopping is affordable. The bottling line is not a bridge to retirement if the bridge ends early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leak-test training require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have to set aside a leaking bottle, mark its batch and show that I can stop the test rig safely. A trainer needs to watch me on guarded equipment during paid hours. I cannot pay fees out of the rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which outside posts would you apply to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A packing posting would have to show real hours and a base wage, and the bus fare must leave enough for rent and food. Leak testing adds the qualification gate. I won't take a dangerous night shift just to say I found a job.

say: **2031 robots** could cap and pack bottles while I am only 63.
The owner should give operators **written shift plans** before cancelling a line.
think: I expect a **major wage loss** from robot bottling.
A few weeks of savings and **irregular shop pay** cannot bridge the years to an affordable stop.
do: **Ask** the owner for written plans and funded paid guarded leak-test training.
**Apply** to real safe local packing or qualified test posts if hours fall and net pay covers rent.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major hour loss and earlier lost sleep over a cancelled batch.
S2.quote: The bottling line is not a bridge to retirement if the bridge ends early.
fieldNote: Her **expected major line loss** and past sleeplessness support alarm, although she is willing to learn quickly.
Outside **packing and testing applications** need posted safe local work and rent-covering net pay; testing also needs completed practical qualification.

steps.text: Enrol in leak testing if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply to posted safe local packing if hours cut and net pay covers rent
Apply to posted safe local testing if qualified, hours cut, net pay covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI can take order planning by 2031, but robots able to handle bottles arrive around 2034. I'd be 66 by then. The three extra years could give me time to learn a second task, provided the line still pays me while I do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband and I need actual figures before I call 67 the finish. I could be one year away and still unable to cover rent without my wage. If the owner offers paid testing work, I would try for it; otherwise a course leaflet is just paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner for a paid guarded leak-testing place and keep notes on the first bad bottles. If the funded place is offered, I'll complete it and have the trainer sign off the practical test. I'll add new wages to our reserve after rent in full weeks. If bottling hours then fall, I'll apply for a posted safe local test role only if qualified and its net pay and travel leave enough for the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the later date gives me a little time to put proof behind a plan. I cannot leave the bottling line on a calendar square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What proof would a leak-test trainer require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to show the trainer I can trace a wet ring back to its batch and stop the rig behind its guard. A paper pass without the practical test would not make me safe. I want the work paid while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the test-role pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The local posting must say its base pay, hours and site. We would subtract travel and compare the remainder with rent, food and the bicycle shop's actual pay. If that doesn't add up, I'll stay on the line while it has hours.

say: **2031 planning AI** comes before bottle-handling robots around 2034.
Three extra years help only if there is **paid work** while I learn.
think: At **66**, rent may still need my line wage.
Age **67** is not an exit until actual household income covers costs.
do: **Train** if a funded paid guarded testing place is offered and signed off.
**Save** new wages; apply to a posted safe local test role only if qualified, hours fall and net pay works.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement affordability, with some time to act.
S3.quote: I cannot leave the bottling line on a calendar square.
fieldNote: Her **testing plan** requires a funded paid guarded place, a practical sign-off and a real posted local role.
The **new reserve deposits** come from full wages after rent; the proposed age 67 stop depends on actual income.

steps.text: Attend leak testing if funded paid guarded place offered
Save new wages from full bottling weeks after rent
Apply to posted safe local testing if qualified, hours fall, net pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family that AI reaches the order desk around 2036, when I am 68, and capable robots the bottling line about 2039, when I am 71. Maybe I can finish work before then. I would rather earn and save than bet the rent on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to stop at 67 in 2035, but I cannot assume any payment at that age. Our current savings barely cover weeks. If documented income after work does not cover the flat and food, I may still be on a line when AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep learning the bottling line and save a little from each full-pay week after rent. My husband and I will write down monthly costs and ask for documented retirement income figures, then decide whether 2035 is affordable. If I am still working after 2036 and hours fall, I'll apply to a posted safe local line or packing role only if its net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money, even with a decade. I can be willing to learn and still need a pay slip on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether 2035 works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would list rent, food and the actual income available after I stop. The number has to cover those bills without pretending the bicycle shop will always be busy. If it does not, 2035 is a year on paper, not a resignation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you seek another line role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the actual posting's hours, safety and bus fare. If I have already stopped with enough income, I will not apply. If I am still working and the line cuts hours, I need a wage that leaves us enough after the journey.

say: **2036 AI** and later robots give time to count costs before making promises.
I would prefer **earned wages** and careful saving to a hoped-for payment.
think: Our **thin savings** cannot cover years of rent without work.
A **2035 stop** depends on actual documented income, and I may still be employed after 2036.
do: **Save** fresh wages after rent and check actual retirement income against monthly costs.
**Apply** only if still employed after 2036, hours fall and a safe local posted role pays enough net.
feel: **Anxious** about the rent despite time to prepare.
S4.quote: I can be willing to learn and still need a pay slip on Friday.
fieldNote: The **retirement figures** are an enquiry, not an entitlement or an actual early exit; 2035 remains conditional.
A **later application** requires continued employment, lost hours and a posted safe local role at bill-covering net pay.

steps.text: Save new wages from full bottling weeks after rent
Compare documented retirement income with monthly rent and food
Apply to posted safe local packing if employed after 2036, hours fall, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 one. I might lose most bottling shifts at 63 before we can afford to stop. I would need written notice, a funded paid guarded test place and posted safe local work with enough pay after travel. My husband and I still need to count the real retirement income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the first spoiled pallet when a new machine misses a loose cap. The soap can be clean and the whole carton still be wet.

headlineQuote: The soap can be clean and the whole carton still be wet.
portrait: **Bianca**, 58, is a junior soap-bottling operator with secondary schooling who uses checked AI explanations every day.
She and her bicycle-repairer husband have **grown children**, low pay, under a month saved and few nearby plants.
Her **traditional outlook** favours earned wages and family help; she is quick to try tools but insists on guarded practical teaching.
She is **alarmed** by expected fast shift loss; a stop at 67 requires documented household income that covers rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may bring bottle-handling robots by 2031, cutting shifts at age 63 before she can afford retirement.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid guarded testing and real safe local posts with adequate net pay would help.
